notes: First-refresh audit, 2026-09-03. The second of the two articles the Phase-B batch scheduling orphaned; it had no ledger. The 2026-08-31 infra session had already removed the "faster process" framing family from the article prose, cache.json and the index card - that removal was re-verified and HOLDS, except in one surface nobody checked: the JSON-LD description still said EPA would "streamline" the exclusions. This audit is close to a rewrite. Four hard errors: the House passage date was April 26 in the article and April 22 in three independent records; the exceptional events rule was cited as 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix A when it is 40 CFR 50.14; the article stated as fact that prescribed burns have an uncertain status under the current rule when 40 CFR 50.14(b)(3) is titled "Prescribed fires" and gives them an express pathway; and the list of documentation the rule requires matched nothing in the rule. Plus a coverage failure: the "What the FIRE Act Would Change" list carried three bullets and omitted the bill's biggest changes, including that the replacement exclusion list drops the current statutory exclusion for high-temperature and lack-of-precipitation events. All positions were removed rather than balanced, because standing rule 7 bars positions outside trackers - and the tracker-conversion option is flagged for James rather than taken. The stored bill text is the INTRODUCED version on a bill that has passed the House; the engrossed text was fetched and diffed this session and is word-for-word identical in its operative provisions, so nothing was analysed against superseded text. ROUND 2 (hostile sonnet pass over the rewritten draft, with the ten-bullet diff re-derived bullet by bullet from the engrossed bill against the current statute): 0 BLOCKING, 6 advisory - and all six were actioned rather than adjudicated away. The one worth recording is the direction claim: the definition bullet was headed "broader" and bundled a clearly broadening addition with the removal of "at a particular location", whose direction no source resolves and which may well narrow that clause. Also fixed: an amendment count that was the article's own bullet count rather than the bill's six instructions, an unledgered "every category" absolute, a dropped precondition on the prescribed-fire practices route, and an EPA source cited on the page but registered on no ledger row. ROUND 3 (a second independent hostile sonnet pass, which rebuilt the ten-bullet diff from the bill and the statute rather than from the ledger): 1 blocking + 5 advisory, and the advisory that mattered most is the one this note exists for. THE 18-MONTH DEADLINE IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE. The bill amends subparagraph (A) of the rulemaking paragraph, which is the PROPOSED-regulations deadline; subparagraph (B) gives EPA a further year after the proposal to promulgate the final rule, and the bill does not touch it. Seven surfaces - lede, bullet, does-not-do section, meta description, og:description, JSON-LD description and index card - all said the bill requires EPA to REVISE its regulations within 18 months. All seven now say propose. It is the same shape as the "faster process" framing this page has already had removed twice: a deadline inside the bill read as a promise about the outcome. Two further defects came from my own re-read rather than the verifier: a dropped condition on the section 110(k)(5) determination, and a nested pair of double quotes that made the NAAQS quotation unreadable. The blocking finding - a stale JSON-LD dateModified - is resolved by the refresh publish, which is what stamps that field. ROUND 4. The third hostile pass came back CLEAN - 0 blocking - having rebuilt the ten-bullet diff from the bill and the statute independently and re-verified the round-3 "propose, not revise" rewrite. Its single advisory was that the sentence "the bill attaches no consequence to EPA missing either of the deadlines it sets" carried no ledger row, which is fair: an absence claim needs a receipt as much as a presence claim does, and the honest receipt for one is the whole amendatory text. That row now exists. Round 4 also carries two fixes from my own re-read AFTER that clean pass, both the dropped-condition class, both in the determination list round 3 had already edited once: item (B) lost "the assignment or re-assignment of a classification category" and its design-values condition, and item (D) named the extension rather than the determination about the data. A clean verifier pass is not the same as a clean article.

claims.claim: The current statutory definition of an exceptional event has four elements, including that it "affects air quality", "is not reasonably controllable or preventable", and "is an event caused by human activity that is unlikely to recur at a particular location or a natural event".
claims.sourceSpan: means an event that— (i) affects air quality; (ii) is not reasonably controllable or preventable; (iii) is an event caused by human activity that is unlikely to recur at a particular location or a natural event;
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: The statute today excludes three things from the definition: stagnation of air masses or meteorological inversions; a meteorological event involving high temperatures or lack of precipitation; and air pollution relating to source noncompliance.
claims.sourceSpan: (i) stagnation of air masses or meteorological inversions; (ii) a meteorological event involving high temperatures or lack of precipitation; or (iii) air pollution relating to source noncompliance.
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: The implementing rule is 40 CFR 50.14, titled "Treatment of air quality monitoring data influenced by exceptional events" - a numbered section, not an appendix.

claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: The rule lists the regulatory determinations excluded data can be kept out of, ending with "Other actions on a case-by-case basis as determined by the Administrator."
claims.sourceSpan: (A) An action to designate an area, pursuant to Clean Air Act section 107(d)(1), or redesignate an area, pursuant to Clean Air Act section 107(d)(3), for a particular national ambient air quality standard; (B) The assignment or re-assignment of a classification category to a nonattainment area where such classification is based on a comparison of pollutant design values, calculated according to the specific data handling procedures in 40 CFR part 50 for each national ambient air quality standard, to the level of the relevant national ambient air quality standard; (C) A determination regarding whether a nonattainment area has attained the level of the appropriate national ambient air quality standard by its specified deadline; (D) A determination that an area has data for the specific NAAQS, which qualify the area for an attainment date extension under the CAA provisions for the applicable pollutant; (E) A determination under Clean Air Act section 110(k)(5), if based on an area violating a national ambient air quality standard, that the state implementation plan is inadequate under the requirements of Clean Air Act section 110; and (F) Other actions on a case-by-case basis as determined by the Administrator.
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: A demonstration must include five listed elements, among them a narrative conceptual model, a clear causal relationship, comparative analyses, a not-reasonably-controllable-and-not-reasonably-preventable showing, and a showing the event was unlikely to recur or was natural.
claims.sourceSpan: The demonstration to justify data exclusion must include: (A) A narrative conceptual model that describes the event(s) causing the exceedance or violation and a discussion of how emissions from the event(s) led to the exceedance or violation at the affected monitor(s); (B) A demonstration that the event affected air quality in such a way that there exists a clear causal relationship between the specific event and the monitored exceedance or violation; (C) Analyses comparing the claimed event-influenced concentration(s) to concentrations at the same monitoring site at other times to support the requirement at paragraph (c)(3)(iv)(B) of this section. The Administrator shall not require a State to prove a specific percentile point in the distribution of data; (D) A demonstration that the event was both not reasonably controllable and not reasonably preventable; and (E) A demonstration that the event was a human activity that is unlikely to recur at a particular location or was a natural event.
claims.section: What the Law Says Now
claims.note: Retyped from "quote" to "definition" in round 2: four of the five elements are quoted verbatim in the prose but the comparative-analyses element is paraphrased, so the row is not a pure quotation row.

claims.claim: FIXED - THE ARTICLE'S CENTRAL FACTUAL CLAIM WAS WRONG, TWICE. It said in its own voice that "Under current rules, prescribed burns occupy an uncertain status - they are human-caused, which creates ambiguity about whether they qualify as exceptional events", and repeated it in the prescribed-burn section. 40 CFR 50.14(b)(3) is titled "Prescribed fires" and provides an express pathway: the Administrator SHALL exclude the data where a State makes the demonstration; there are two named routes to the not-reasonably-controllable test; there is a Table 1 of basic smoke management practices; and there is a post-burn review requirement. The uncertainty framing is a position held on the floor by supporters, not a fact about the regulation, and this article is not a tracker, so it is removed rather than attributed. The section is rewritten from the regulation.
claims.sourceSpan: (3) Prescribed fires. (i) The Administrator shall exclude data from use in determinations of exceedances and violations, where a State demonstrates to the Administrator's satisfaction that emissions from prescribed fires caused a specific air pollution concentration in excess of one or more national ambient air quality standards at a particular air quality monitoring location and otherwise satisfies the requirements of this section.
claims.section: Prescribed Burns Are Already in the Rule
claims.note: The floor record shows the same point contested: the sponsor addressed the argument "that this bill is unnecessary because there is already enough flexibility under the Clean Air Act for exceptional events and prescribed burns", and a named opponent said "The Clean Air Act already allows States to submit data for air pollution caused by exceptional events". Both are in data/cr-cache/119-HR-6387.txt. Neither is used in the article, because attributing positions outside a tracker is barred.

claims.claim: FIXED. The article said states "must submit detailed documentation - meteorological data, fire location data, dispersion modeling, and statistical analysis - demonstrating that the fire caused the exceedance and that the exceedance would not have occurred absent the fire". The rule lists five elements and requires "a clear causal relationship between the specific event and the monitored exceedance or violation". Both the list and the standard are replaced with the regulation's own text.

claims.claim: FIXED - POSITIONS REMOVED BECAUSE THIS IS NOT A TRACKER. The article carried a one-sided "What Sponsors Say Is Wrong With the Current Process" section and a lede paragraph asserting what sponsors argue, while its meta description promised "what sponsors argue, what opponents say, and how the House voted" and its index card asserted "opponents say it would weaken the NAAQS program" - a position sourced to nothing, the residue of a removed Earthjustice attribution. HANDOFF standing rule 7 bars positions, characterisations and analysis outside trackers, and docs/BOTH-SIDES.md puts both-sides content only inside a tracker. The bill would meet the both-sides ELIGIBILITY triggers (a 220-198 recorded vote and on-record statements from named members, all in data/cr-cache/119-HR-6387.txt), so converting this page into a tracker is a real option - but that is a scope decision for James, not something to do inside an audit. Every position is removed from the article, the meta and og descriptions, and the index card, and the article is now structural throughout.

claims.claim: The bill is six numbered amendatory instructions, all to section 319(b).
claims.sourceSpan: Section 319(b) of the Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7619(b)) is amended-- (1) in the subsection heading, by inserting ``Or Actions To Mitigate Wildfire Risk'' after ``Events''; (2) in paragraph (1)-- (A) in the paragraph heading, by striking ``Definition of exceptional event'' and inserting ``Definitions''; (B) in subparagraph (A), by redesignating clauses (i) through (iv), as subclauses (I) through (IV), respectively; (C) by striking ``(A)'' and all that follows through ``an event that--'' and inserting the following: ``(A) Exceptional event.-- ``(i) In general.--The term `exceptional event' means an event that--''; (D) by amending subclause (III) of subparagraph (A)(i), as redesignated, to read as follows: ``(III) is an event that is-- ``(aa) a natural event; ``(bb) caused by a human activity that is intended to mirror the occurrence or reoccurrence of a natural event; or ``(cc) caused by a human activity that is unlikely to recur; and''; (E) by striking subparagraph (B) and inserting the following: ``(ii) Exclusions.--In this subsection, the term `exceptional event' does not include-- ``(I) ordinarily occurring stagnation of air masses; ``(II) meteorological inversions; or ``(III) air pollution relating to source noncompliance.''; and (F) by adding at the end the following: ``(B) Action to mitigate wildfire risk.--The term `action to mitigate wildfire risk' means a prescribed fire or similar measure, undertaken in accordance with State approved practices, to reduce the risk and severity of wildfires.''; (3) in paragraph (2)-- (A) in subparagraph (A)-- (i) by striking ``March 1, 2006'' and inserting ``18 months after the date of enactment of the FIRE Act''; (ii) by inserting ``revisions to'' before ``regulations''; and (iii) by adding ``or actions to mitigate wildfire risk'' before the period at the end; (B) in subparagraph (B)-- (i) by inserting ``including proposed revisions to regulations,'' after ``subparagraph (A),''; (ii) by inserting ``or action to mitigate wildfire risk'' after ``an exceptional event''; and (iii) by striking ``paragraph (3)'' and inserting ``this section''; and (C) by adding at the end the following: ``(C) Regional analysis.--When more than one State notifies the Administrator of its intent to submit a petition pursuant to this section for an exceptional event or an action to mitigate wildfire risk for the same air quality event, or, if the Administrator determines such a multistate air quality event has occurred, the Administrator shall conduct regional modeling and analysis sufficient to satisfy the demonstration required for an exceptional event or an action to mitigate wildfire risk petition for such air quality event. ``(D) Transparency.--Not later than 12 months after the date of enactment of the FIRE Act, the Administrator shall establish, and thereafter update monthly, a public website describing the status of all petitions submitted pursuant to this section for exceptional events and actions to mitigate wildfire risk.''; (4) in paragraph (3)(A)-- (A) by redesignating clauses (ii) through (v) as clauses (iii) through (vi), respectively; and (B) by inserting after clause (i) the following: ``(ii) the principle that actions to mitigate wildfire risk can play an important role in reducing the magnitude and frequency of wildfires;''; (5) in paragraph (3)(B)-- (A) in clause (i), by inserting ``or action to mitigate wildfire risk'' before ``must be''; (B) by amending clause (ii) to read as follows: ``(ii) a clear causal relationship must exist, or be reasonably expected to exist, between the measured exceedances of a national ambient air quality standard and the exceptional event or action to mitigate wildfire risk to demonstrate that the exceptional event or action to mitigate wildfire risk caused a specific air pollution concentration at a particular air quality monitoring location;''; and (C) by amending clause (iv) to read as follows: ``(iv) there are criteria and procedures for the Governor of a State to petition the Administrator to exclude air quality monitoring data that is directly due to exceptional events or actions to mitigate wildfire risk from use in determinations by the Administrator with respect to-- ``(I) area or source exceedances or violations of the national ambient air quality standards; ``(II) the designation, redesignation, classification, or reclassification of an area; ``(III) the demonstration by a State of attainment of a national ambient air quality standard; ``(IV) attainment determinations; ``(V) attainment date extensions; ``(VI) finding a State implementation plan to be inadequate; or ``(VII) preconstruction demonstrations under section 165(a)(3).''; and (6) by striking paragraph (4).
claims.section: What the FIRE Act Would Change
claims.note: The receipted span runs from the amending clause to the last instruction and contains all six, numbered (1) through (6). The article breaks them into ten bullets for the reader; the count of instructions in the bill is six, and the prose now says six.

claims.claim: Section 319(b) is not limited to wildfire: its definition of an exceptional event turns on whether an event affects air quality, is not reasonably controllable or preventable, and is natural or unlikely to recur.
claims.sourceSpan: means an event that— (i) affects air quality; (ii) is not reasonably controllable or preventable; (iii) is an event caused by human activity that is unlikely to recur at a particular location or a natural event;

claims.claim: The basic-smoke-management-practices route carries a further condition: the state, federal land managers and other entities as appropriate must periodically collaborate with burn managers and document the process.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 2 - A DIRECTION ASSERTED THAT NO SOURCE SUPPORTS. The bullet was headed "A broader definition of exceptional event" and then described two changes: the new (bb) clause, which is unambiguously broadening, and the removal of "at a particular location" from the unlikely-to-recur clause, whose direction is genuinely unresolved - the old test asked whether an event was unlikely to recur AT THAT LOCATION, which is easier to satisfy than unlikely to recur at all. Bundling them under "broader" implied both cut the same way. The bullet is now headed "A new category in the definition of exceptional event", says clause (bb) is new, and says of the location words that "nothing in the bill says which way that cuts, and neither does the statute."

claims.claim: The 18-month deadline lands on the PROPOSED regulations. The statute still gives EPA one year after publishing the proposal to promulgate the final regulations, and the bill does not touch that.
claims.sourceSpan: (B) Final regulations Not later than 1 year after the date on which the Administrator publishes proposed regulations under subparagraph (A), and after providing an opportunity for interested persons to make oral presentations of views, data, and arguments regarding the proposed regulations, the Administrator shall promulgate final regulations
claims.section: What the FIRE Act Would Change
claims.note: The bill amends subparagraph (A), which is the PROPOSED-regulations deadline ("Not later than March 1, 2006 ... the Administrator shall publish in the Federal Register proposed regulations"). Its only edit to subparagraph (B) is to insert "including proposed revisions to regulations," and the wildfire phrase - the one-year clock is untouched. So the outer bound on a completed rulemaking is roughly 30 months, not 18.

claims.claim: The determination list includes a section 110(k)(5) finding that a state implementation plan is inadequate, but only if based on an area violating a standard.
claims.sourceSpan: (E) A determination under Clean Air Act section 110(k)(5), if based on an area violating a national ambient air quality standard, that the state implementation plan is inadequate
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: EPA describes the six as pollutants "which can be harmful to public health and the environment".
claims.sourceSpan: which can be harmful to public health and the environment.

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 3 - AN 18-MONTH DEADLINE THAT IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE, ON FOUR SURFACES. The lede, the change bullet, the "What the Bill Does Not Do" section, the meta description, the og:description, the JSON-LD description and the index card all said the bill requires EPA to REVISE its regulations within 18 months. The bill amends subparagraph (A), which is the PROPOSED-regulations deadline; subparagraph (B) separately gives EPA a year after the proposal is published to promulgate the final regulations, and the bill leaves that clock alone. So 18 months is the deadline to PROPOSE, and a completed rulemaking could run to about 30 months. Every one of the seven surfaces now says propose. This is the same shape as the "faster process" family this page has already had removed twice: a deadline in the bill being read as a promise about the outcome.
claims.sourceSpan: (A) Proposed regulations Not later than March 1, 2006, after consultation with Federal land managers and State air pollution control agencies, the Administrator shall publish in the Federal Register proposed regulations governing the review and handling of air quality monitoring data influenced by exceptional events.
claims.section: What the FIRE Act Would Change

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 3 - A DROPPED CONDITION I FOUND ON MY OWN RE-READ, NOT FROM THE VERIFIER. The list of regulatory determinations rendered item (E) as "findings that a state implementation plan is inadequate". The rule reads "A determination under Clean Air Act section 110(k)(5), IF BASED ON AN AREA VIOLATING A NATIONAL AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARD, that the state implementation plan is inadequate" - the condition is what ties the determination to the air-quality data the section is about, and without it the item reads as covering any SIP-inadequacy finding. Restored, with the statutory hook named.
claims.sourceSpan: (E) A determination under Clean Air Act section 110(k)(5), if based on an area violating a national ambient air quality standard
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 3 - NESTED DOUBLE QUOTES, found on my own re-read. The NAAQS sentence quoted a stretch of EPA prose that itself contains a quoted term, so the rendered page read: ... for six principal pollutants ( "criteria" air pollutants ) which can be ... inside an outer pair of double quotes, with the source page's own stray spacing carried through. A reader cannot tell where the quotation starts or stops. Rebuilt as two short quoted fragments with the parenthetical as the article's own prose.
claims.sourceSpan: requires EPA to set National Ambient Air Quality Standards (40 CFR part 50) for six principal pollutants ( "criteria" air pollutants ) which can be harmful to public health and the environment.
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: RESOLVED AT PUBLISH, ROUND 3. The verifier graded it blocking that the JSON-LD dateModified read 2026-07-17 while the visible meta line and the status paragraph both said September 2026 - the structured data contradicting the prose a crawler reads next to it. That contradiction is transient by design: publish-article --refresh is what stamps dateModified, and hand-editing it in the draft would put the wrong number in the file the publish script then overwrites. It is stamped 2026-09-03 by the refresh publish that ships this audit. Also actioned: the transition sentence "What the bill changes is the terms on which it operates" sat immediately after the CFR mechanics and could be read as saying the bill edits the rule, when it edits the statute the rule implements - now said in terms; and three ledger rows typed "quote" over prose that paraphrases rather than quotes were retyped to "definition".

claims.note: AN ABSENCE CLAIM, so the receipt is the WHOLE amendatory text rather than a passage inside it - the span runs from the amending clause to the last of the six instructions and therefore contains every operative word the bill enacts. Verified by reading it end to end: neither the 18-month proposal deadline nor the 12-month website deadline is followed by any penalty, forfeiture, deemed-approval, reporting-to-Congress or cause-of-action clause, and the bill creates no enforcement provision of any kind. The 119-HR-6387 cache entry records the same absence in its gaps[] field.

claims.claim: The classification determination is the assignment or re-assignment of a classification category to a nonattainment area, and only where the classification rests on a comparison of pollutant design values.

claims.claim: The attainment-date-extension item is a determination that an area has data qualifying it for the extension, not the extension itself.
claims.sourceSpan: (D) A determination that an area has data for the specific NAAQS, which qualify the area for an attainment date extension
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 4 - TWO MORE COMPRESSED CONDITIONS IN THE SAME LIST, FOUND ON MY OWN RE-READ AFTER A CLEAN PASS. Round 3 restored the section 110(k)(5) condition to item (E) of the determination list and left the neighbouring items alone. Item (B) was rendered "classification of a nonattainment area", dropping both "the assignment or re-assignment of a classification category" and the condition "where such classification is based on a comparison of pollutant design values" - so it read as covering any classification of any nonattainment area. Item (D) was rendered "attainment date extensions", which names the outcome; the rule's item is "A determination that an area has data for the specific NAAQS, which qualify the area for an attainment date extension" - a determination about the DATA. Both restored. The list was internally inconsistent as well as imprecise: two items were quoted with their conditions and two were summarised past them.
claims.sourceSpan: (B) The assignment or re-assignment of a classification category to a nonattainment area where such classification is based on a comparison of pollutant design values, calculated according to the specific data handling procedures in 40 CFR part 50 for each national ambient air quality standard, to the level of the relevant national ambient air quality standard;
claims.section: What the Law Says Now

claims.claim: FIXED, ROUND 5 - ONE WORD. The article said of the final-regulations stage that "The second stage is untouched". Its CLOCK is untouched, but subparagraph (B) is not: the bill makes three insertions into it - "including proposed revisions to regulations," after "subparagraph (A),", "or action to mitigate wildfire risk" after "an exceptional event", and "this section" for "paragraph (3)". None of them moves the one-year deadline, which is the claim the sentence is making, but "untouched" said more than that. Now "The second stage's clock is untouched".
